title: Random Walks and Gambler's Ruin
objectives: Model a bankroll as a random walk with absorbing barriers at 0 and a target N
Derive the gambler's ruin probability $u_i$ from the one-step difference equation, for both fair and biased walks
Compute how a small house edge collapses the probability of reaching a target, with exact numbers
Connect the ruin formula to risk of ruin for a trader and to bet sizing
motivation: A trading account is a random walk with an absorbing barrier at zero: one path of wins and losses, and ruin is the state you never come back from. The gambler's ruin formulas quantify what intuition misses badly - how a tiny edge against you, compounded over many bets, turns a 10% shot at doubling into under 1%, and how bankroll size (not just skill) controls survival.

blocks.text: A bankroll is a random walk

blocks.md: Bet \$1 at a time on a game you win with probability $p$ and lose with probability $q = 1-p$. Your bankroll $X_t$ then performs a random walk on the integers: each step is $+1$ with probability $p$ and $-1$ with probability $q$. Two states are **absorbing**: $0$ (ruin - no money to bet) and $N$ (your target, at which you stop). Starting from $i$, the two questions that matter are: what is the probability of reaching $N$ before $0$, and how long does the game last? The walk picture makes 'risk of ruin' concrete - every losing streak is just a downward segment of the path, and the question is whether the path hits zero before it ever touches the target.

blocks.caption: Paths of a p = 0.49 walk starting at 10 with absorbing barriers at 0 and 100. Watch how few paths ever reach 100 - and how many end absorbed at 0.

blocks.md: Let $u_i$ be the probability of reaching $N$ before $0$ when starting from bankroll $i$. The boundaries are $u_0 = 0$ and $u_N = 1$. Conditioning on the **first** step - the same first-step analysis used throughout probability - gives a difference equation, because after one bet the problem restarts from a neighbouring bankroll.

blocks.title: Solve the difference equation
items: Guess a solution of the form $u_i = x^i$. Substituting: $x^i = p x^{i+1} + q x^{i-1}$, i.e. $p x^2 - x + q = 0$.
The quadratic factors as $(x - 1)(px - q) = 0$, so the roots are $x = 1$ and $x = q/p$.

**Biased case** ($p \ne q$): the general solution is $u_i = A + B\,(q/p)^i$. The boundaries give $A + B = 0$ and $A + B (q/p)^N = 1$, so $B = \tfrac{1}{(q/p)^N - 1}$ and $u_i = \tfrac{(q/p)^i - 1}{(q/p)^N - 1}$.
**Fair case** ($p = q = \tfrac{1}{2}$): the roots coincide, and the solution is linear - second differences vanish - so $u_i = i/N$: your success probability is literally your share of the target.

blocks.caption: Probability of reaching N before 0, starting from i.

blocks.md: Sanity checks: $u_0 = 0$ and $u_N = 1$ in both branches; for $p = \tfrac{1}{2}$ the formula is symmetric under $i \leftrightarrow N - i$, as it must be. A fair gambler with \$10 chasing \$100 succeeds exactly $10/100 = 10\%$ of the time - your probability of doubling is your edge in units over the house's head start.

blocks.text: Fair versus biased: the edge compounds

blocks.md: Now watch what a genuinely small disadvantage does. Take $p = 0.49$, start $i = 10$, target $N = 100$. Then $q/p = 51/49 \approx 1.0408$; over 100 units of distance that factor compounds: $(51/49)^{100} \approx 54.6$. Plugging in: $u_{10} = \tfrac{1 - 1.492}{1 - 54.6} \approx 0.0092$ - under **1%**, versus 10% for the fair game. A 2% per-bet disadvantage did not shave 2% off your chances; it divided them by eleven, because the ratio $q/p$ is exponentiated by the distance to the target.

Duration behaves the same way. For the fair walk the expected number of bets to absorption is $E[T] = i(N - i)$, so $10 \to 100$ takes **900 bets on average** - long, but finite. For $p = 0.49$ the expectation is $E[T] = \tfrac{i - N u_i}{q - p} = \tfrac{10 - 100 \times 0.0092}{0.02} \approx 454$ bets, most of them ending at zero. Real casinos work the same arithmetic in reverse: European roulette (win on red with $p = \tfrac{18}{37}$) gives a \$100 gambler chasing \$200 a success probability of $\tfrac{1 - (19/18)^{100}}{1 - (19/18)^{200}} \approx 0.45\%$.

blocks.caption: A Monte Carlo check of the closed form: simulation reproduces 0.92% and 10%.

blocks.text: Risk of ruin for a trader

blocks.md: Flip the perspective: a trader with a genuine edge has $p > \tfrac{1}{2}$, and the relevant question is the probability of ever hitting zero when there is no upper target ($N \to \infty$). Letting $N$ grow in the formula, with $q/p < 1$ now, gives $u_i \to 1 - (q/p)^i$, so the **risk of ruin** is $P(\text{ruin}) = (q/p)^{i}$ - decaying geometrically in your bankroll measured in bet sizes. With $p = 0.55$: starting at $i = 10$ units, ruin risk is $(9/11)^{10} \approx 13.4\%$; at $i = 20$ units it is $(9/11)^{20} \approx 1.8\%$. Note the squares: **doubling your bankroll squares your ruin probability**, which is why sizing, not just edge, is the survival lever.

blocks.title: The martingale betting scam, audited by the formula
blocks.md: Double your stake after every loss so the first win recovers everything. To survive $n$ consecutive losses you need $1 + 2 + 4 + \dots + 2^{n-1} = 2^n - 1$ units - 127 units for a 7-loss streak - all to win a single unit. The ruin formula says why it fails: with $p \le \tfrac{1}{2}$ the walk reaches 0 eventually with probability near 1, so the 'sure thing' is a lottery ticket on not seeing a normal losing streak before the table limit.

blocks.title: Positive edge does not immunise you
blocks.md: $P(\text{ruin}) = (q/p)^i$ is small only when $i$ (bankroll in bet units) is large relative to the edge. Halve the bet size - double $i$ - and you square the survival odds; double the bet size and you square the ruin odds upward. Over-betting a profitable strategy is the classic way a desk with a real edge still blows up.

guidedExercise.prompt: Derive $u_i = i/N$ for the **fair** walk ($p = q = \tfrac{1}{2}$) directly from the difference equation: show the gaps $d_i = u_i - u_{i-1}$ must be constant, then apply the boundaries.
hints: Write the fair-case equation $u_i = \tfrac{1}{2}u_{i+1} + \tfrac{1}{2}u_{i-1}$ and move terms around until it says something about $u_{i+1} - u_i$ versus $u_i - u_{i-1}$.
If all gaps are equal to some constant $c$, then $u_i = c \cdot i$.
guidedExercise.solution: Multiplying $u_i = \tfrac{1}{2}u_{i+1} + \tfrac{1}{2}u_{i-1}$ by 2 and rearranging: $u_{i+1} - u_i = u_i - u_{i-1}$, so every gap $d_i = u_i - u_{i-1}$ equals the same constant $c$. Then $u_i = u_0 + c\,i = c\,i$ using $u_0 = 0$. The boundary $u_N = 1$ forces $c = \tfrac{1}{N}$, hence $u_i = \textbf{i/N}$. Example: $i = 10$, $N = 100$ gives $0.1$ - a fair gambler's chance of reaching the target equals their share of it.

independentExercise.prompt: A gambler starts with $20 and aims to reach $50, betting \$1 per hand with win probability $p = 0.45$. (a) Compute the probability of reaching the target exactly, using the ruin formula with $q/p = 11/9$. (b) Compare with the fair-game answer and comment on the size of the gap.
hints: The fair answer needs no formula: $u_i = i/N$.
independentExercise.solution: (a) $r^{20} = e^{20 \times 0.2007} \approx 55.3$ and $r^{50} = e^{50 \times 0.2007} \approx 22{,}800$, so $u_{20} = \tfrac{1 - 55.3}{1 - 22{,}800} = \tfrac{54.3}{22{,}799} \approx \textbf{0.0024}$ - about $0.24\%$. (b) The fair game gives $u_i = 20/50 = 40\%$. A mere 5-point edge against the gambler cut the chance of reaching the target by a factor of about 170 - the ratio $q/p$ is raised to the power of the distance to the target, so small edges compound brutally.

commonMistakes: Using $i/N$ for biased walks - the linear formula holds only when $p = \tfrac{1}{2}$; otherwise the exponential form with $q/p$ applies.
Mixing up the numerator and denominator in $\tfrac{1 - (q/p)^i}{1 - (q/p)^N}$: the exponent $i$ (start) belongs on top, $N$ (target) below.
Reading a 49% game as 'almost fair': over a 90-unit climb the success probability drops by a factor of about 11.
Computing risk of ruin for a favorable game with the target formula instead of the limit $(q/p)^i$ as $N \to \infty$.
Forgetting that expected duration for the fair walk is $i(N-i)$, not $N$ - a fair \$10-to-\$100 gambler sits at the table ~900 bets on average.
realWorldApplication: The ruin framework is the backbone of risk limits: position-sizing rules that keep bankroll (capital) large in units of per-trade risk are direct applications of $P(\text{ruin}) = (q/p)^i$, and the same absorption mathematics describes corporate cash reserves hitting zero.
quantFinanceApplication: Desk risk committees translate the ruin formula into limits: with win rate $p$ and per-trade risk $b$, capital $C$ supports $i = C/b$ units, and $P(\text{ruin}) = (q/p)^{C/b}$ decays geometrically in $C/b$ - the quantitative argument behind fixed-fractional sizing and maximum-drawdown kill switches.
summary: A bankroll is a random walk with absorbing barriers at 0 (ruin) and N (target); first-step conditioning gives $u_i = p\,u_{i+1} + q\,u_{i-1}$ with $u_0 = 0$, $u_N = 1$.
Solution: $u_i = \tfrac{1-(q/p)^i}{1-(q/p)^N}$ when $p \ne \tfrac{1}{2}$, and $u_i = i/N$ for a fair game - so fair \$10-to-\$100 success is exactly 10%.
Small edges compound: at $p = 0.49$ the same \$10-to-\$100 quest succeeds only ~0.92% (and ~0.04% at $p = 0.48$), because $(q/p)^{N-i}$ decays exponentially in the distance to target.
Fair-game expected duration is $E[T] = i(N-i)$ - 900 bets for 10-to-100; the biased walk ends sooner and almost always at zero.

With an edge and no upper target, risk of ruin is $(q/p)^i$: doubling bankroll squares the ruin probability, so bet sizing is the survival lever, and martingale doubling fails because a $2^n - 1$ bankroll still faces a near-certain 0.

quiz.prompt: A fair game ($p = 0.5$): starting bankroll \$10, target \$100, \$1 bets. What is the probability of reaching \$100 before ruin?
Same stakes but $p = 0.49$. Using $q/p = 51/49$, compute $u_{10}$ for $N = 100$ (as a decimal to four places).
quiz.explanation: $u_{10} = \tfrac{1 - (51/49)^{10}}{1 - (51/49)^{100}} = \tfrac{1 - 1.492}{1 - 54.6} \approx 0.0092$: the tiny edge collapses a 10% chance to under 1%.

quiz.prompt: For the fair walk starting at $i = 10$ with target $N = 100$, the expected number of bets until the walk is absorbed (at 0 or 100) is:
quiz.explanation: $E[T] = i(N - i) = 10 \times 90 = 900$. A fair gambler takes a surprisingly long time to reach either barrier - the walk is recurrent and drifts nowhere.

quiz.prompt: A trader has edge $p = 0.55$ and no upper target. Which statement about risk of ruin $P(\text{ruin}) = (q/p)^{i}$ is TRUE?
options: It decreases linearly as bankroll grows
Doubling the bankroll (in bet units) squares the ruin probability
It depends only on p, not on bankroll
It equals $i/N$ for any target N
quiz.explanation: $(q/p)^{2i} = \left((q/p)^{i}\right)^2$: geometric decay means doubling capital squares the ruin odds. With $p = 0.55$: 13.4% at $i = 10$ versus 1.8% at $i = 20$.

quiz.prompt: A gambler plays a perfectly fair game ($p = 0.5$) forever, with no target: they keep betting \$1 against an infinitely rich casino. What is the probability they are eventually ruined, and why (one or two sentences)?
quiz.modelAnswer: The probability is 1. A one-dimensional symmetric random walk is recurrent: with no upper barrier ($N \to \infty$) the success probability $u_i = i/N$ tends to 0, so the walk visits 0 eventually with certainty.
quiz.explanation: $u_i = i/N \to 0$ as the target $N \to \infty$, so ruin is certain: a fair game against an unlimited house is a slow, sure death march - the walk returns to every level, including 0, with probability 1.

quiz.prompt: What does this Python code print?
quiz.explanation: $r = 1.5$, so $r^{50}$ is astronomically large while $r^{5} = 7.59$; the success probability is about $1.0 \times 10^{-8}$, which rounds to $0.0$ at four decimals. With a 10% edge against you, turning \$5 into \$50 is effectively impossible.

flashcards.back: $u_i = \dfrac{1 - (q/p)^{i}}{1 - (q/p)^{N}}$ for reaching $N$ before $0$ starting at $i$, with $q = 1 - p$.
$u_i = i/N$: your chance of reaching the target equals your bankroll's share of it. \$10 to \$100 in a fair game = exactly 10%.

flashcards.front: Risk of ruin with a positive edge and no upper target
flashcards.back: $P(\text{ruin}) = (q/p)^{i}$, with $i$ = bankroll in bet units. Doubling bankroll squares the ruin probability.

flashcards.front: Why does a tiny house edge collapse long-shot goals?
flashcards.back: The ratio $q/p$ (slightly > 1) is raised to the power of the distance between start and target: at $p = 0.49$, $(51/49)^{100} \approx 55$ compounds across a \$10-to-\$100 climb, shrinking a 10% fair-game shot to about 0.9%.

flashcards.front: Spot the error: 'Martingale doubling is safe because the first win always recovers all losses.'
flashcards.back: Surviving n losses requires $2^n - 1$ units (127 for n = 7) to win 1, and with $p \le 1/2$ the ruin formula says hitting 0 is near-certain on long horizons - the table limit or bankroll does the absorbing.
